released_bridges.name: Euclidean norms and Lipschitz continuity
released_bridges.content_boundary: Interpret Euclidean norms and a Lipschitz bound for a vector-valued gradient; exclude function-value Lipschitzness.

learning_outcomes.text: Compute the Euclidean norm of a vector and use it to measure the distance between two vectors.
Read a vector-valued Lipschitz inequality as a bound on output change relative to input change.
Apply that interpretation when the vector-valued map is a gradient, without confusing it with function-value Lipschitzness.

teaching_content.text: For z in R^d, the Euclidean norm is ||z||_2 = sqrt(z^T z), and ||x-y||_2 measures Euclidean distance between x and y.
For L>0 and all x,y in the domain, a vector-valued map G is L-Lipschitz when ||G(x)-G(y)||_2 <= L||x-y||_2. The inequality bounds output-vector change by input-vector change.
When G is the gradient map, compare the norm of the gradient difference with the norm of the point difference. This concerns changes in gradient vectors, not a bound on |f(x)-f(y)|.
For G(x)=2x, ||G(x)-G(y)||_2 = 2||x-y||_2, so the Lipschitz inequality holds with L=2. The example concerns a vector map only and introduces no gradient-descent claim.

excluded_content: The Descent Lemma or its proof

released_bridges.name: Inner products and convex sets
released_bridges.content_boundary: Interpret convex combinations and first-order inner-product inequalities; exclude advanced convex analysis.

learning_outcomes.text: Compute an inner product and recognize that its result is a scalar.
Form a convex combination and use it to recognize the defining closure property of a convex set.
Parse an expression of the form g^T(y-x) as an inner product with a displacement vector, without asserting an optimisation theorem.

teaching_content.text: For real vectors u and v of the same dimension, u^T v is the scalar sum of their componentwise products.
For x and y and a scalar theta in [0,1], theta x + (1-theta)y is a convex combination. A set is convex when it contains this combination for every pair of its points and every such theta.

To read g^T(y-x), first form the displacement d=y-x and then compute the scalar inner product g^T d. The sign describes alignment of g and the displacement; no convexity conclusion follows from this computation alone.
For x=(0,0)^T, y=(2,4)^T, and theta=1/4, theta x+(1-theta)y=(3/2,3)^T. If g=(1,-1)^T, then g^T(y-x)=-2. These are arithmetic interpretations, not a first-order convexity theorem.

Proofs of convexity or global optimality
Subgradients, separation theorems, and other advanced convex analysis

released_bridges.name: Ratios and condition numbers
released_bridges.content_boundary: Compute and interpret L/mu and the lower bound kappa>=1; exclude other condition measures.

learning_outcomes.text: Compute kappa=L/mu for positive constants with L>=mu.
Interpret kappa as the multiplicative separation between L and mu without importing another condition-number definition.

teaching_content.text: For constants 0<mu<=L, define the condition ratio kappa=L/mu.
Because mu is positive, dividing 0<mu<=L by mu gives kappa=L/mu>=1. A value near 1 means the two constants are close; a larger value means they are more widely separated multiplicatively.
If L=12 and mu=3, then kappa=4, so L is four times mu. If L=mu, then kappa=1.
The ratio requires mu>0. Do not treat L/mu as a finite condition ratio when mu=0.

excluded_content: Matrix, spectral, or numerical linear-algebra condition numbers
Step-size selection, acceleration, or stochastic optimisation claims
